summary: Mangal Yatra ("Mars Journey") is a helmet-mounted heads-up display that puts a layered Martian map directly in an astronaut's line of sight during a Marswalk. We built a web map of Jezero Crater that combines several NASA missions: MRO CTX and HiRISE imagery, MGS MOLA elevation with computed slope, CRISM mineral maps, and the Perseverance rover traverse. On top of it we planned an EVA route with waypoints, distances, slope and boulder hazards, and resource targets. The HUD shows a route arrow, distance to the next waypoint, hazard warnings and mock suit telemetry. Head tracking from an Arduino Nicla Sense ME turns the map as the astronaut turns, and on-device voice commands ("next waypoint", "show hazards", "return to base") keep hands free. Everything runs locally on a Raspberry Pi 5 with no Earth link. Mars has no GPS or global magnetic field, so position is simulated along the route and we describe how real systems would use orbiter fixes, visual odometry and gyro data. Mangal Yatra turns separate datasets into one actionable view for planning and safely carrying out a surface excursion.
details:
What it does: Mangal Yatra is a Martian survival map delivered through a helmet HUD. It answers the challenge by integrating data from multiple NASA missions into one layered view of Jezero Crater and one planned EVA route, so an astronaut can see terrain, hazards, resources and the way home at the same time.

Data layers: MRO CTX and HiRISE imagery for terrain, MGS MOLA elevation with slope computed using GDAL (slopes above roughly 15 to 20 degrees flagged), HiRISE rock hazards, Perseverance (Mars 2020) landing site and traverse as ground truth, MRO CRISM mineral maps for hydrated-mineral resource targets, and environment context from Perseverance MEDA. All layers were reprojected to one Mars coordinate system, tiled with gdal2tiles and exported as GeoJSON for the route, waypoints, hazards and resources.

HUD and hardware: The HUD is a single web page (Leaflet/MapLibre) with a dark high-contrast theme, route arrow, distance to next waypoint, hazard alerts, layer toggles and mock suit telemetry. It runs in Chromium kiosk mode on a Raspberry Pi 5 (8GB). An Arduino Nicla Sense ME streams heading over USB to a Python WebSocket service so the map rotates with the wearer's head, and also supplies mock suit readings (temperature, humidity, air quality). Voice control uses Vosk offline speech recognition with a fixed command list (next waypoint, show hazards, show resources, return to base, zoom). The image is shown on a small display reflected in a beam splitter in front of the eyes. A keyboard-controlled version runs in any laptop browser.

Mars realities: There is no GPS or global magnetic field on Mars, so position is simulated along the route, and we describe how real systems would combine visual odometry, gyro data and orbiter fixes. Everything runs on-device with no Earth link.

Benefits and impact: One glanceable, hands-free view reduces the need to consult separate maps and lowers the risk of walking into slope or boulder hazards, supporting safer and more efficient surface excursions.

Tools: Python, JavaScript, Leaflet/MapLibre, GDAL, Arduino C++, Vosk, Raspberry Pi OS.

Creativity: we combine real multi-mission NASA data with wearable AR-style hardware and offline voice control, built in one weekend.

Factors considered: hardware failure fallbacks, readability on a beam splitter (bright lines on black), power and heat inside a helmet, and honest handling of Mars-specific navigation limits.
